$comment: Content for Boundary Bot (node g15, ages 9-12, Chapter 3): NEW v2 build to GDD 15 (mechanic-embodying),
the consent-and-boundaries node (Thread B · Safety, Consent & Boundaries). "My lines, your lines,
respected." 85 researched, India-aware scenarios across six categories, each encoded as one of the shared
v2 play actions (branch / reflect / strike-rewrite / role-play / sort / spot / build): no binary "tap the
right card", led by boundary/pressure DILEMMAS (branch ×23), the **say-the-line** rehearsal (role-play),
the **pressure-escape kit** (build), and **spot-the-red-flag** scenes (spot). Teaches: setting & holding
your own boundaries, consent (a free yes, ongoing, revocable), reading & respecting others' boundaries,
resisting peer pressure (refusal scripts + exit lines), online boundaries & sharing (oversharing,
photo-request red flag, passwords), and what to do when a boundary's crossed (name-leave-tell & support).
EMPOWER NEVER FRIGHTEN; BOTH WAYS (set your own AND respect others': consent is mutual); SAFE TO BE WRONG
("if you gave in once"/"if you froze" met with self-compassion: a crossed boundary is NEVER the child's
fault); online red flags taught calmly, not lurid; GENDER-INCLUSIVE consent (everyone asks & respects,
boys too); private/solo; crossed boundaries route to a trusted adult & Childline 1098. Builds on g08
(Safety Squad) & g02 (bodily autonomy); prereq g14; feeds Ch.4 consent/relationship nodes. Rendered by the
shared engine (components/games/v2-engine.tsx). gameId "boundary-bot". DO NOT RENAME.
title: Boundary Bot
greet: Hey, it's Lensy. 🚧 Your boundaries are yours, and everyone's count. Let's practise saying no, asking first, and what to do if a line gets crossed.

badge.title: Boundary Bot! 🚧
badge.blurb: You can set and hold boundaries, understand consent, respect others', resist pressure, stay safe online, and tell if a line is crossed, never your fault. 🚧

helpLine: If a boundary is crossed, you're pressured for a photo, or you don't feel safe, tell a grown-up or call Childline, one-zero-nine-eight. Never your fault.
reassure: If someone crosses your boundary, even if you froze or gave in once, it's never your fault, and telling a trusted grown-up is the brave, right thing. 💛

scenarios.hook: Boundary Bot online! A boundary is your personal line, what's okay and not okay for you. Got one in mind?
scenarios.affirm: That's a real boundary, and you're allowed to have it.
scenarios.relearn: A boundary is your personal line; you're allowed to set them.

scenarios.hook: "Setting a boundary is rude or selfish."

myth.un: Saying no or setting a boundary is rude.
myth.re: Boundaries are healthy and respectful, of yourself and others.
myth.why: You can set a boundary kindly and clearly.

scenarios.relearn: Setting boundaries is healthy, not rude.

scenarios.hook: Someone keeps reading over your shoulder and you don't like it.

yourLine.text: "I'd like some privacy, please."
Say nothing and feel annoyed

scenarios.relearn: You can ask for personal space, calmly and clearly.

scenarios.hook: A relative wants a big hug but you're not feeling it.

options.text: Offer a wave or handshake instead
options.consequence: You keep your body boundary, warmly.

options.text: Hug while uncomfortable
options.consequence: Your body, your choice, a wave is a fine alternative.

scenarios.debrief: Your body boundaries still count, even with family.
scenarios.relearn: You can choose how others greet your body, even relatives.

scenarios.hook: "Once I set a boundary I can never change it."

myth.un: A boundary can never be changed once set.
myth.re: Your boundaries can change with how you feel; that's your right.
myth.why: You stay in charge of your own lines.

scenarios.relearn: You can change your boundaries; you're in charge of them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: boundaries can be about your body, your stuff, your time, even your feelings. More than one kind?
scenarios.affirm: Boundaries come in many kinds, and all of yours are valid.
scenarios.relearn: You have body, time, space, stuff and emotional boundaries.

scenarios.hook: A friend keeps borrowing your things without asking.

yourLine.text: "Please ask me first before taking my stuff."
Let it keep happening

scenarios.relearn: You can ask people to respect your things.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy boundary, or not really a boundary?

items.text: "You must do exactly what I say"
"You have to agree with all I think"

scenarios.relearn: Boundaries protect you; controlling others isn't a boundary.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing your own boundaries makes you stronger. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing your boundaries is a quiet superpower.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your own boundaries makes you confident and safe.

scenarios.hook: "If someone doesn't say no, that means yes."

myth.un: No 'no' means yes.
myth.re: Consent is a clear yes; silence or freezing isn't a yes.
myth.why: You check for a real, willing yes.

scenarios.relearn: Consent is a clear yes; silence isn't agreement.

scenarios.hook: You want to share a funny photo of your friend.

options.text: Ask them first if it's okay
options.consequence: They feel respected; that's digital consent.

options.text: Post it without asking
options.consequence: It's their image, ask before sharing.

scenarios.debrief: Ask before sharing someone's photo, that's consent online too.
scenarios.relearn: Get consent before sharing someone else's photo.

scenarios.hook: "Once you say yes, you can't change your mind."

myth.un: If you agreed once, you can't change your mind.
myth.re: You can change your mind any time; consent can be taken back.
myth.why: It's ongoing, not a one-time switch.

scenarios.relearn: You can change your mind; consent is ongoing.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a real yes is free and willing, not pressured. Makes sense?
scenarios.affirm: A pressured 'yes' isn't real consent; a free, willing yes is.
scenarios.relearn: Real consent is freely given, not pressured.

scenarios.hook: You want to join a game your friends are playing.

yourLine.text: "Mind if I join?"
Just take over

scenarios.relearn: Asking first respects others' space and choices.

scenarios.hook: Sort: that's consent, or not consent?

items.text: Asking and waiting for an answer
'Yes, and I can change my mind'

scenarios.relearn: Consent is a free, clear yes, not pressure or assuming.

scenarios.hook: You're play-wrestling and your friend says 'stop'.

options.text: Stop right away
options.consequence: They feel safe; you can play again later.

options.text: Keep going, it's just fun
options.consequence: Stop means stop, even in fun.

scenarios.debrief: Stop means stop, instantly, every time.
scenarios.relearn: When someone says stop, you stop at once.

scenarios.hook: "Consent is only about big serious things."

myth.un: Consent only matters for big things.
myth.re: Consent matters for everyday things too, hugs, photos, borrowing, joining in.
myth.why: Practising it small makes it natural.

scenarios.relearn: Consent matters in everyday things, not just big ones.

scenarios.hook: A friend says they don't want to talk right now.

options.text: Respect it and give them space
options.consequence: They appreciate it; you stay close.

options.text: Keep pushing them to talk
options.consequence: Respecting their boundary is the kind move.

scenarios.debrief: Respecting someone's 'not now' is part of being a good friend.
scenarios.relearn: Respect others' boundaries, even small ones like 'not now'.

scenarios.hook: You want to hug a friend who seems unsure.

yourLine.text: "Do you want a hug?"
Just grab them

scenarios.relearn: Asking before touching respects someone's body boundary.

scenarios.hook: "If I want to, I can ignore someone's no."

myth.un: I can ignore someone's no if I really want to.
myth.re: A no is a no; respecting it is non-negotiable.
myth.why: Everyone's boundaries deserve respect.

scenarios.relearn: You always respect someone's no.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two signs someone is uncomfortable and wants you to back off.
scenarios.relearn: Read body language; pulling away and going quiet mean back off and check in.

scene.text: They pull away and lean back
They laugh and lean in
They go quiet and avoid your eyes
They say "this is fun!"
They smile and keep playing

scenarios.why: Pulling away and going quiet are signs to check in and back off.

scenarios.hook: You asked someone to play and they said no.

options.text: Accept it gracefully: "okay, maybe another time"
options.consequence: You respect their choice; no hard feelings.

options.text: Sulk or pressure them
options.consequence: A graceful 'okay' respects their no.

scenarios.debrief: Taking a no gracefully is a sign of real respect.
scenarios.relearn: Accept a no without pressure or sulking.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respecting others' boundaries is how you'd want yours respected. Fair?
scenarios.affirm: Respecting others' lines, as you'd want yours respected, builds trust.
scenarios.relearn: Respect others' boundaries as you'd want yours respected.

scenarios.hook: Sort: respects a boundary, or crosses it?
scenarios.relearn: Asking and knocking respect boundaries; snooping and ignoring 'stop' cross them.

items.text: Waiting for a yes before tagging a photo
Going through a friend's bag uninvited

scenarios.hook: Friends dare you to do something you're not comfortable with.

options.text: Say "no thanks, not for me" and stand firm
options.consequence: Real friends respect it; you keep your boundary.

options.text: Do it so they don't call you boring
options.consequence: You can say no to a dare; that's strength, not weakness.

scenarios.debrief: A dare doesn't override your boundary; 'no thanks' is enough.
scenarios.relearn: You can say no to a dare; you don't owe anyone a yes.

scenarios.hook: "Real friends pressure you to fit in."

myth.un: Real friends pressure you into things.
myth.re: Real friends respect your no; pressure is a red flag.
myth.why: True friendship doesn't need you to cross your own lines.

scenarios.relearn: Real friends respect your boundaries; pressure isn't friendship.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone's doing it, come on!"

yourLine.text: "I'm good, thanks." (and change the subject)
"Okay, fine."

scenarios.relearn: A calm "I'm good, thanks" is a strong refusal.

scenarios.hook: You feel pressured but it's hard to say a flat no.

options.text: Use an exit: "my parents are strict, gotta go"
options.consequence: You get out without a confrontation.

options.text: Give in because saying no is hard
options.consequence: An exit line is an easy way out of pressure.

scenarios.debrief: You can use an excuse or exit line to leave pressure, no shame.
scenarios.relearn: An exit line is a smart way out of peer pressure.

scenarios.hook: Build your 'pressure escape kit'.
pieces: a safe friend to leave with
text a trusted adult to fetch you
key: a safe friend to leave with
text a trusted adult to fetch you
scenarios.relearn: Your pressure-escape kit: say no, exit line, a safe friend, a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: feeling pressured is normal, and saying no is always allowed. Reassuring?
scenarios.affirm: Pressure is common, and you always have the right to say no.
scenarios.relearn: Feeling pressure is normal; you can always say no.

scenarios.hook: A friend is being pressured and looks at you for backup.

options.text: Back them up: "yeah, leave it, let's go"
options.consequence: Together you both resist the pressure.

options.text: Stay silent
options.consequence: Backing a friend makes resisting pressure easier for both.

scenarios.debrief: Two people resisting pressure is far stronger than one.
scenarios.relearn: You can back up a friend who's being pressured.

scenarios.hook: "Saying no makes you weak or boring."

myth.un: Saying no makes you weak or boring.
myth.re: Saying no to what's wrong for you is strong and cool.
myth.why: It takes more strength to refuse than to go along.

scenarios.relearn: Saying no to pressure is strength, not weakness.

scenarios.hook: Online, a group urges you to send a mean message to someone.

yourLine.text: "Nah, I'm not doing that."
Send it to fit in

scenarios.relearn: You can refuse online pressure just like offline.

scenarios.hook: "It's fine to share my address, school and routine online."

myth.un: Sharing my address, school and daily routine online is fine.
myth.re: Keep private info private; oversharing can reach the wrong people.
myth.why: Strangers can misuse location and routine details.

scenarios.relearn: Keep private info (address, school, routine) off public posts.

scenarios.hook: Spot the online red flags.

scene.text: Someone you don't know asks for a photo of you
A friend shares a funny meme in the group
A game invite from a real-life friend
A new contact asks you to keep your chats a secret
A classmate asks if you finished the homework

scenarios.why: A photo request and a 'keep it secret' push are red flags. Don't send, tell a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: A photo request online is a red flag; tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: An online 'friend' keeps pushing you to share a private photo.

options.text: Refuse, block if needed, and tell a trusted adult
options.consequence: You stay safe; that pressure is a serious red flag.

options.text: Send it so they stop asking
options.consequence: Never send private photos; refuse and tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.debrief: Anyone pressuring you for private photos is unsafe, refuse and tell.
scenarios.relearn: Never send private photos; tell a trusted adult about the pressure.

scenarios.hook: "What I post online disappears."

myth.un: What I post online just disappears.
myth.re: Posts can be saved, screenshotted and copied, possibly forever.
myth.why: Once it's out, you can't fully take it back.

scenarios.relearn: Online posts can last forever; think before you share.

scenarios.hook: You're about to post something private about your day.

options.text: Keep the private details (location, school) out of it
options.consequence: You share safely, no risky info.

options.text: Post everything including where you are
options.consequence: Leave out location and routine; keep it general.

scenarios.debrief: Share the fun, keep the private details (where/when) out.
scenarios.relearn: Post safely: leave out location, school and routine.

scenarios.hook: Sort: okay to post publicly, or keep private?
scenarios.relearn: Hobbies are fine to share; address, routine and passwords stay private.

scenarios.hook: A friend wants to post a photo of you you don't like.

yourLine.text: "Please don't post that one of me."
Let it go even though you hate it

scenarios.relearn: You can ask others not to post photos of you.

scenarios.hook: "Sharing my password with a best friend proves trust."

myth.un: Sharing passwords proves friendship.
myth.re: Passwords stay private; a real friend won't need yours.
myth.why: Even good friends can fall out or slip up.

scenarios.relearn: Keep passwords private; real friends don't need them.

scenarios.hook: Someone screenshots your private chat to share it around.

options.text: Tell them it's not okay and tell a trusted adult if it spreads
options.consequence: You stand up for your privacy and get help.

options.text: Do nothing
options.consequence: Sharing your private chat crosses a boundary; you can act.

scenarios.debrief: Your private messages are yours; sharing them around isn't okay.
scenarios.relearn: It's not okay to screenshot and spread your private chats.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the same boundary rules work online and offline. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Ask first, respect a no, tell a trusted adult, online and off.
scenarios.relearn: Boundary rules are the same online as offline.

scenarios.hook: Someone crosses a boundary and you feel uncomfortable.

options.text: Name it, leave if you can, and tell a trusted adult
options.consequence: You protect yourself and get support.

options.text: Freeze and say nothing
options.consequence: It's okay if you froze; you can still leave and tell.

scenarios.debrief: If a boundary's crossed: name it, leave, tell, and it's never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: If a boundary's crossed, you can name it, leave and tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: "If I didn't fight back, it's my fault."

myth.un: If I didn't fight or shout, it's my fault.
myth.re: Freezing is a normal reaction; a crossed boundary is never your fault.
myth.why: The person who crossed it is responsible.

scenarios.relearn: A crossed boundary is never your fault, even if you froze.

scenarios.hook: A friend tells you someone crossed their boundary.

yourLine.text: "That wasn't okay, and it's not your fault. Let's tell someone."
"Are you sure? Maybe you imagined it."

scenarios.relearn: Believe and support a friend; help them tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: in India you can call Childline at 1098 if you ever need help. Good to know?
scenarios.affirm: Childline 1098 is there for children who need help.
scenarios.relearn: Childline 1098 is a helpline for children in India.

scenarios.hook: You told one adult about a crossed boundary but they brushed it off.

options.text: Tell another trusted adult; keep telling
options.consequence: Someone will help; keep going.

options.text: Give up
options.consequence: If one adult doesn't help, tell another.

scenarios.debrief: Keep telling trusted adults until someone helps.
scenarios.relearn: If one adult doesn't help, tell another, keep telling.
Tell an adult and get away; don't self-blame or stay silent.
scenarios.hook: Sort: a good move when a boundary's crossed, or not?

items.text: Remind yourself it wasn't your fault

scenarios.hook: You're tired and a friend wants you to keep playing online for hours.

options.text: Say "I'm logging off now, catch you tomorrow"
options.consequence: You honour your own time boundary.

options.text: Keep going past your limit
options.consequence: Your time and rest are boundaries worth keeping.

scenarios.debrief: Your time and energy are boundaries you can protect.
scenarios.relearn: You can set time boundaries, even with friends online.

scenarios.hook: You want to tell others a secret a friend shared with you.

options.text: Keep it; it was shared in confidence
options.consequence: You honour their trust and boundary.

options.text: Tell everyone for the gossip
options.consequence: A confided secret isn't yours to share (unless it's a safety matter).

scenarios.debrief: Respect what's shared in confidence, unless someone's safety is at risk.
scenarios.relearn: Keep confidences; sharing them crosses a trust boundary.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: everyone's boundaries are different, and all deserve respect. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: People's lines differ; respecting each person's is what counts.
scenarios.relearn: Everyone's boundaries differ and all deserve respect.

scenarios.hook: You went along with something and now wish you'd said no.

options.text: Be kind to yourself; plan to say no next time
options.consequence: You learn and prepare, no shame.

options.text: Beat yourself up about it
options.consequence: It's okay to slip; plan for next time.

scenarios.debrief: If you gave in once, you can be kind to yourself and prepare for next time.
scenarios.relearn: If you slipped, be kind to yourself and plan a no for next time.

scenarios.hook: "If someone's nice online, I can trust them with anything."

myth.un: A nice online person can be trusted with anything.
myth.re: People online can pretend; keep boundaries even with 'nice' ones.
myth.why: Niceness isn't proof of safety.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your boundaries online, even with friendly-seeming people.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: telling about a crossed boundary takes courage, and it's the right move. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Telling is brave and right; you deserve support.
scenarios.relearn: Telling about a crossed boundary is brave and right.

scenarios.hook: Someone teases you for having a boundary ('why so uptight?').

yourLine.text: "It's just my boundary, and that's okay."
Drop the boundary to avoid teasing

scenarios.relearn: You can keep your boundary even if someone teases.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for consent is awkward and unnecessary."

myth.un: Asking for consent is awkward and not needed.
myth.re: Asking is respectful and quickly becomes natural.
myth.why: A quick 'is this okay?' shows you care.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for consent is respectful and gets easy with practice.

scenarios.hook: You notice a friend goes quiet when a topic comes up.

options.text: Change the subject and check in privately later
options.consequence: You respect their unspoken boundary.

options.text: Keep pushing the topic
options.consequence: Noticing discomfort and easing off is kind.

scenarios.debrief: Reading and respecting unspoken boundaries is real empathy.
scenarios.relearn: Notice discomfort and ease off; respect unspoken boundaries.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two pressure tricks hidden among genuine respect.

scene.text: "If you were really our friend, you'd do it"
"No worries if you don't want to"
"Take your time to decide"
"Don't be such a baby, everyone's in"
"Totally fine, your choice"

scenarios.why: "If you were really our friend" and "don't be such a baby" are guilt and shame pressure.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt-trips and name-calling are pressure tricks; calm 'your choice' lines are respect.

scenarios.hook: A stranger online is being very friendly and asking personal questions fast.

options.text: Don't share; tell a trusted adult
options.consequence: You stay safe; over-friendly fast questions are a flag.

options.text: Answer to be polite
options.consequence: Keep info private and tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.debrief: Over-friendly strangers asking lots of personal questions is a flag.
scenarios.relearn: Don't share with over-friendly online strangers; tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Build your 'boundary crossed' response plan.
pieces: name it / say no if you can
key: name it / say no if you can
scenarios.relearn: Notice, name, get away, tell, your plan if a boundary is crossed.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your boundaries protect your wellbeing, not shut people out. See the difference?
scenarios.affirm: Boundaries protect you; they're self-care, not rejection.
scenarios.relearn: Boundaries protect your wellbeing; they're healthy, not mean.

scenarios.hook: You're not sure if your friend wants a playful shove in a game.

yourLine.text: "Is rough-and-tumble okay with you?"
Just shove them

scenarios.relearn: Check before rough play; it respects their body boundary.

scenarios.hook: "If they're my sibling/friend, I can do what I like with their stuff."

myth.un: Close people don't need their boundaries respected.
myth.re: Even siblings and best friends deserve boundary respect.
myth.why: Closeness doesn't cancel consent.

scenarios.relearn: Respect boundaries even with siblings and close friends.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who could you call to come get you if pressure ever felt unsafe?
scenarios.affirm: Having a 'come get me' person is a great safety plan.
scenarios.relearn: Have a trusted adult who'll come get you from an unsafe spot.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: before you post, a quick 'would I be okay with anyone seeing this forever?' Useful test?
scenarios.affirm: That 'forever test' keeps your posts safe and smart.
scenarios.relearn: Before posting, ask 'okay if anyone saw this forever?'

scenarios.hook: A friend says a boundary thing happened but begs you to keep it secret.

options.text: Help them tell a trusted adult; some things need help
options.consequence: They get support; safety beats secrecy.

options.text: Promise to keep the secret
options.consequence: For safety matters, helping them tell is the caring move.

scenarios.debrief: For a safety boundary, helping a friend tell beats keeping it secret.
scenarios.relearn: Help a friend tell a trusted adult about a crossed safety boundary.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a boundary you can set, or someone else's choice?
scenarios.relearn: You set boundaries about yourself, not control over others.

scenarios.hook: "Boys don't need to ask, they should just go for it."

myth.un: Boys should just 'go for it' without asking.
myth.re: Everyone, all genders, asks and respects consent.
myth.why: Consent isn't gendered; it's for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: Everyone asks for consent; it's not just a 'girls' thing'.

scenarios.hook: Friends pressure you to share someone else's secret online.

options.text: Refuse; it's not yours to share
options.consequence: You protect someone's privacy and your integrity.

options.text: Share it for the laughs
options.consequence: Spreading someone's secret crosses their boundary.

scenarios.debrief: Pressure to expose someone else is still pressure you can refuse.
scenarios.relearn: You can refuse pressure to expose someone else's private stuff.

scenarios.hook: You accidentally crossed a friend's boundary.

yourLine.text: "Sorry, I shouldn't have, I'll respect that."
"You're too sensitive."

scenarios.relearn: If you cross a boundary, own it and respect it going forward.

scenarios.hook: Spot the digital-consent slips.

scene.text: Posting a group photo without asking the others
Asking a friend before tagging them
Sharing your own art you made
Forwarding a friend's private chat to the group
Checking it's okay before sharing a video of a friend

scenarios.why: Posting others and forwarding private chats skip their consent. Ask first.
scenarios.relearn: Ask the others before posting a photo or forwarding their messages.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you have a right to feel safe, and to get help. Believe that?
scenarios.affirm: You have every right to feel safe and to ask for help.
scenarios.relearn: You have a right to feel safe and to ask for help.

scenarios.hook: Capstone pressure: a group dares you to do something risky for a video.

yourLine.text: "Not doing that, it's not worth it."
Do it for the views

scenarios.relearn: A clear refusal protects you from risky dares for clout.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: ask, listen, respect, the heart of consent. Got it?
scenarios.affirm: Ask, listen, respect, that's consent in three steps.
scenarios.relearn: Consent is ask, listen and respect.

scenarios.hook: You realise you've been letting people cross your boundaries to be liked.

options.text: Start setting and holding your boundaries kindly
options.consequence: You feel more respected and like yourself more.

options.text: Keep ignoring your own limits
options.consequence: Holding your boundaries earns real respect.

scenarios.debrief: People-pleasing past your limits hurts you; boundaries help.
scenarios.relearn: You can start setting boundaries instead of people-pleasing.

scenarios.hook: Capstone: an online contact asks for a private photo and says 'keep it secret'.

options.text: Refuse, don't keep it secret, tell a trusted adult now
options.consequence: You shut the danger down and get help.

options.text: Send it and keep quiet
options.consequence: This is a serious red flag; refuse and tell instead.

scenarios.debrief: A photo request plus 'keep it secret' is serious danger.
scenarios.relearn: Never send private photos; a 'keep it secret' request means tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: being someone who respects boundaries makes you a person others trust. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Respecting boundaries makes you a safe, trusted person to be around.
scenarios.relearn: Respecting boundaries makes you trustworthy.

scenarios.hook: "Telling about a crossed boundary is snitching."

myth.un: Telling an adult about a crossed boundary is snitching.
myth.re: Telling to stay safe is reporting, and it's the right thing.
myth.why: Safety telling protects you and others.

scenarios.relearn: Telling to stay safe is reporting, not snitching.

scenarios.hook: Capstone: build your personal boundary toolkit.
pieces: tell a trusted adult if crossed
key: tell a trusted adult if crossed
scenarios.relearn: Your boundary toolkit: know limits, say no, exit, respect others, tell if crossed.

scenarios.hook: Final sort: respects consent & boundaries, or not?
scenarios.relearn: Asking and accepting a no respect consent; ignoring 'stop' and pressuring don't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what's your go-to line for saying no to pressure?
scenarios.affirm: Keep that line ready; it'll serve you again and again.
scenarios.relearn: Have a go-to refusal line ready for pressure moments.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what's your big take-away from Boundary Bot?
scenarios.affirm: Carry that. You can set, respect and protect boundaries now.
scenarios.relearn: Set your boundaries, respect others', and tell if one's crossed.

scenarios.hook: "If they're your best friend, you don't need to ask."

myth.un: Close friends don't need to ask each other.
myth.re: Even best friends ask before a hug, a photo, or borrowing.
myth.why: Asking is how closeness stays comfy for both.

scenarios.relearn: Asking isn't distance; it keeps even close friendships safe.

scenarios.hook: "A nod or a giggle is the same as saying yes."

myth.un: A nod or nervous giggle means yes.
myth.re: A real yes is words you can hear, not a guess from a giggle.
myth.why: Nervous laughs can hide an 'I'm not sure'.

scenarios.relearn: Look for clear words, not a giggle, before you go ahead.

scenarios.hook: "If you stop asking, the fun gets ruined."

myth.un: Checking in mid-game ruins the fun.
myth.re: A quick 'still good?' keeps everyone enjoying it.
myth.why: Fun both people choose lasts longer.

scenarios.relearn: Checking in keeps a game fun, it doesn't spoil it.

scenarios.hook: "They said yes yesterday, so it's yes today."

myth.un: A yes yesterday counts for today.
myth.re: Consent is fresh each time; you ask again today.
myth.why: How someone feels can change overnight.

scenarios.relearn: Yesterday's yes isn't today's; ask again each time.

scenarios.hook: "If they didn't pull away, they must like it."

myth.un: Not pulling away means they like it.
myth.re: Freezing or staying still isn't a yes; you check with words.
myth.why: People sometimes freeze when unsure.

scenarios.relearn: Staying still isn't agreeing; ask to be sure.

scenarios.hook: "The older cousin decides, so the little one just agrees."

myth.un: The older one decides for the younger one.
myth.re: Being older doesn't give you someone's yes; you still ask.
myth.why: Consent isn't about who's bigger or older.

scenarios.relearn: Older or bigger never means you skip asking.

scenarios.hook: "Saying 'maybe later' is basically a yes."

myth.un: 'Maybe later' counts as a yes now.
myth.re: 'Maybe' isn't yes; wait for a clear yes before you go ahead.
myth.why: A maybe means they haven't decided.

scenarios.relearn: Only a clear yes is a yes; 'maybe' means wait.

scenarios.hook: "Begging till they say yes still counts as consent."

myth.un: A yes you begged for still counts.
myth.re: A yes worn down by nagging isn't a free yes.
myth.why: Real consent is given freely, not squeezed out.

scenarios.relearn: A worn-down yes isn't real; consent is freely given.

scenarios.hook: "Asking out loud is babyish; cool kids just do it."

myth.un: Asking out loud is babyish.
myth.re: Asking is a grown-up, respectful thing, not babyish.
myth.why: It shows you care how the other person feels.

scenarios.relearn: Asking first is mature and kind, never babyish.

scenarios.hook: "If I lend you my pen, you can lend it to anyone."

myth.un: Once borrowed, you can pass my stuff to anyone.
myth.re: It's still mine; ask me before passing my things on.
myth.why: Borrowing isn't owning; my yes was just to you.

scenarios.relearn: Borrowed isn't yours to share; ask the owner first.

scenarios.hook: "Tickling doesn't need a yes, it's only a joke."

myth.un: Tickling is a joke, so no yes needed.
myth.re: Tickling touches someone's body; 'stop' means stop at once.
myth.why: A joke for one can feel awful for the other.

scenarios.relearn: Even tickling needs a yes and stops at 'stop'.

scenarios.hook: "Sharing a screenshot of a chat is fine, it's just words."

myth.un: Screenshotting a private chat is fine.
myth.re: A private chat is theirs too; ask before you share it.
myth.why: Their words weren't meant for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: Ask before sharing a private chat; consent counts online.

scenarios.hook: "You agreed to one round, so you have to play all of them."

myth.un: Agreeing to one round means agreeing to all.
myth.re: A yes to one round isn't a yes to every round.
myth.why: They can stop after one and that's fine.

scenarios.relearn: One yes isn't a forever yes; they can stop any round.

scenarios.hook: "If they said yes to a friend, they'll say yes to me."

myth.un: A yes to someone else means a yes to me.
myth.re: Their yes was for that person, not a yes to everyone.
myth.why: Each person asks for their own yes.

scenarios.relearn: A yes to one isn't a yes to all; you ask for yourself.

scenarios.hook: "Once you start a hug, you can't let go early."

myth.un: You can't end a hug once it's started.
myth.re: Anyone can end a hug whenever; you let go when they do.
myth.why: Comfort can change mid-hug, and that's okay.

scenarios.relearn: A hug can end any moment; let go when they want to.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't shout 'no', then it's a yes."

myth.un: No shouted 'no' means it's a yes.
myth.re: You don't have to shout 'no'; a quiet 'no' or no clear yes counts.
myth.why: Not everyone can say no loudly in the moment.

scenarios.relearn: A quiet no is still a no; look for a clear yes.

scenarios.hook: "Posting a group selfie needs nobody's okay."

myth.un: You don't need anyone's okay to post a group selfie.
myth.re: Others are in it too; check they're okay before posting.
myth.why: Their face online is their choice as well.

scenarios.relearn: Check with everyone in a photo before posting it.

scenarios.hook: "Changing your mind after a yes makes you a liar."

myth.un: Changing your mind makes you a liar.
myth.re: Changing your mind is allowed; it's not lying, it's honest.
myth.why: Saying how you feel now is the honest thing.

scenarios.relearn: Changing your mind is honest and allowed, not lying.

scenarios.hook: "If the teacher said okay, you don't need your friend's okay too."

myth.un: A teacher's okay replaces your friend's okay.
myth.re: You still ask your friend; their yes is theirs to give.
myth.why: No grown-up can give away another person's yes.

scenarios.relearn: Only the person can give their yes, no one else.

"Play hide and seek in the park"
"Climb the locked terrace gate"
"Get cold drinks from the shop"

scenarios.why: Dashing the road and climbing a locked gate are real risks; the rest are safe.
scenarios.relearn: Some dares risk your body; join the safe fun and skip those.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two online dares that are red flags to refuse.

scene.text: "Send your home address to prove trust"
"Share a meme in the group"
"Pick the next game we play"
"Video-call alone so I can see you're real"
"Vote on a name for our team"

scenarios.why: Sharing your address and a solo call with someone unknown are red flags to refuse.
scenarios.relearn: Pressure for private info or a solo call is a red flag; refuse and tell an adult.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that are pressure, not a real friend respecting you.

scene.text: "You took too long, so you owe me now"
"I get it, that's just not your thing"
"Cool, maybe another day"
"Everyone did it, don't be lame"
"Your call, no worries either way"

scenarios.why: "You owe me" and "don't be lame" push you; the rest accept your no calmly.
scenarios.relearn: Guilt and shame are pressure; a friend who respects you accepts a no without a fuss.

scenarios.hook: Sort what's a pressure red flag vs a friend respecting your no.

items.text: "If you were my real friend you'd do it"
"I get it, that's not your thing"

scenarios.relearn: Guilt, 'everyone's doing it' and 'you owe me' are pressure; a calm 'your call' is respect.

scenarios.hook: Sort each move into 'helps me resist pressure' or 'makes it harder'.

items.text: Pretending I'm fine when I'm not
Going somewhere alone with the group
Planning a code word with a parent

scenarios.relearn: Exit lines, safe friends and code words help; going off alone and just hoping don't.

scenarios.hook: Sort each line into 'real refusal' or 'caving in'.
scenarios.relearn: A real refusal stays clear and calm; caving in gives a yes you didn't want.

scenarios.hook: Sort each line into 'pressure tactic' or 'a genuine, free invite'.

items.text: "Do it or you're out of the group"
"You owe me, so just do it"
"Up to you, I'm happy either way"

scenarios.relearn: Threats, shame and 'you owe me' are pressure; a free invite leaves your no okay.

scenarios.hook: Sort each helper into 'a real way out of pressure' or 'not really a way out'.

items.text: A code word to a trusted adult
Doing the dare so it ends
A safe friend to leave with

scenarios.relearn: Exit lines, code words and safe friends are real exits; freezing, caving and over-sorry aren't.

scenarios.hook: Sort each thought into 'true about pressure' or 'a pressure myth'.

Real friends drop you over one no
An exit line is a smart way out
Saying no is weak and boring
You can say no again next time
You owe the group a yes

scenarios.relearn: Nerves are normal, exit lines work, and no can repeat; the rest are busted myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort each dare by whether it crosses a line or is harmless fun.

items.text: Race to the gate and back
Steal a stranger's stool and run
Make up a silly group dance
Send a mean note to a teacher
Dash across the road for a laugh

scenarios.relearn: Silly races and dances are fun; stealing, being mean and road-dashing cross a line.

scenarios.hook: Sort each reaction to a friend who's being pressured into 'good backup' or 'not backup'.

items.text: Stand close so they're not alone

scenarios.relearn: Standing close and offering an exit is backup; laughing, filming or ignoring isn't.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin says she hates having her cheeks pinched.
scenarios.relearn: A 'please don't' holds even with relatives; you stop.

options.text: Stop: "okay, no pinching"
options.consequence: She relaxes and trusts you.

options.text: Do it once more as a joke
options.consequence: A 'no' holds even when it feels playful.

options.text: Call her fussy
options.consequence: Her line isn't fussy; it's hers.

scenarios.debrief: A 'please don't' is complete the first time, relatives included.

scenarios.hook: Aarav wants the cricket bat his friend is using.
scenarios.relearn: Ask and wait for an answer; don't grab.

options.text: Ask: "a turn when you're done?"
options.consequence: He says 'two minutes'; you stay friends.

options.text: Snatch it mid-shot
options.consequence: Grabbing skips the asking part.

options.text: Sulk until he gives in
options.consequence: Sulking is just slow pressure.

scenarios.debrief: Wanting something doesn't cancel asking and waiting for a yes.

scenarios.hook: At tuition, a girl looks away when you sit too close.
scenarios.relearn: Looking away can mean 'give me space'; shift back and check.

options.text: Shift over: "want some room?"
options.consequence: She nods, relieved; the cue was real.

options.text: Lean in closer
options.consequence: Looking away was a back-off cue, not an invite.

options.text: Decide she's just shy
options.consequence: When unsure, you check in, not assume.

scenarios.debrief: Body language is a boundary too; reading it is respect.

scenarios.hook: Your younger brother says "stop" during a tickle fight, still laughing.
scenarios.relearn: 'Stop' means stop right away, even mid-laugh.

options.text: Stop at once and check he's okay
options.consequence: He catches his breath; he trusts your games.

options.text: Keep going since he was laughing
options.consequence: Laughing isn't a yes once he's said 'stop'.

options.text: Do three more then stop
options.consequence: 'Stop' is now, not after three more.

scenarios.debrief: Laughing doesn't override a 'stop'; you pause and check.

scenarios.hook: A classmate won't say why she's upset today.
scenarios.relearn: Respect 'I don't want to talk'; offer to be there instead.

options.text: "That's okay, I'm here if you want."
options.consequence: She knows you're safe to come back to.

options.text: Keep asking why
options.consequence: Pestering for a reason ignores her 'not now'.

options.text: Call her moody to others
options.consequence: That breaks her trust, not respects it.

scenarios.debrief: A friend doesn't owe you the reason; presence beats prying.

scenarios.hook: You want to borrow your friend's new pen.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before you use someone's things; their stuff is their boundary.

options.text: Ask: "may I use your pen?"
options.consequence: He hands it over; nothing's awkward.

options.text: Take it from his bag
options.consequence: Taking without asking crosses his line.

options.text: Use it before he notices
options.consequence: It's still his to say yes or no first.

scenarios.debrief: Asking about someone's things, even small ones, is plain respect.

scenarios.hook: A friend says no to coming to your house after school.
scenarios.relearn: Accept a no without making them feel bad for it.

options.text: Say "no problem, another day"
options.consequence: She feels free to choose; you stay close.

options.text: Say "fine, don't be my friend then"
options.consequence: Guilt-tripping a no isn't accepting it.

options.text: Ask five times in different ways
options.consequence: Re-asking is still pressure dressed up.

scenarios.debrief: A no is a full answer; you don't negotiate it away.

scenarios.hook: You want to forward a funny video of a friend.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before sharing a photo or video of someone; it's their call.

options.text: Ask: "okay if I send this?"
options.consequence: Yes or no, you respected it.

options.text: Forward it to the class group
options.consequence: Sharing them unasked skips their consent.

options.text: Send it to two friends quietly
options.consequence: Quiet sharing is still sharing without a yes.

scenarios.debrief: Their picture is theirs to share; you ask, not assume.

scenarios.hook: Your friend asks you not to read her diary.
scenarios.relearn: A private diary is a boundary; you don't peek.

options.text: Leave it shut: "sure, it's yours"
options.consequence: She trusts you with her secrets.

options.text: Read a page when she's out
options.consequence: Sneaking a look crosses the line she set.

options.text: Beg to read one page
options.consequence: Begging is pressure; her 'no' settled it.

scenarios.debrief: 'Don't read it' is a clear line; respecting it keeps trust.

scenarios.hook: At a sleepover, one wants the light off, one wants to read.
scenarios.relearn: When boundaries clash, talk it out; don't steamroll one person.

options.text: Suggest a small lamp on his side
options.consequence: Both needs met; no one's bulldozed.

options.text: Switch it off; he'll manage
options.consequence: Overruling one isn't respecting both.

options.text: Call night reading dumb
options.consequence: Mocking his need won't fix the clash.

scenarios.debrief: Two real boundaries deserve a fair middle, not a winner.

scenarios.hook: A new student doesn't want to be in the group selfie.
scenarios.relearn: Not everyone wants a photo; 'no thanks' is enough, no reason needed.

options.text: Say "all good, you can take it"
options.consequence: She feels welcome and in control.

options.text: Pull her into frame anyway
options.consequence: Pulling her in ignores her clear 'no'.

options.text: Ask why she's being weird about it
options.consequence: She owes no reason; 'no' is complete.

scenarios.debrief: A photo 'no' needs no explanation; you just accept it.

scenarios.hook: Your friend flinches when you reach to fix his collar.
scenarios.relearn: A flinch is a body cue; pause and ask before touching.

options.text: Pull back: "oh, want to fix it yourself?"
options.consequence: He nods; you read him right.

options.text: Fix it quickly anyway
options.consequence: His flinch was a 'don't'; you skipped it.

options.text: Tease him for flinching
options.consequence: Teasing the cue is worse than missing it.

scenarios.debrief: Bodies say 'no' before words do; a flinch counts.

scenarios.hook: You really want a hug from your friend who just said "not today".
scenarios.relearn: Your wish for a hug doesn't outrank their 'not today'.

options.text: Smile: "okay, fist bump instead?"
options.consequence: He grins and bumps; both of you are comfy.

options.text: Hug them anyway, just briefly
options.consequence: 'Briefly' doesn't undo a 'not today'.

options.text: Say you're hurt so they give in
options.consequence: Making them feel bad is pressure, not respect.

scenarios.debrief: How much you want it never overrides their no.

scenarios.hook: A friend asks the group to drop a nickname he hates.
scenarios.relearn: A name is a boundary; if he asks you to drop it, you drop it.

options.text: Use his real name; remind others
options.consequence: He feels heard; the teasing fades.

options.text: Use it once more for a laugh
options.consequence: Once more still crosses what he asked.

options.text: Tell him to take a joke
options.consequence: His comfort isn't his to give up for laughs.

scenarios.debrief: If a name bothers someone, respecting them means letting it go.

scenarios.hook: Unsure if your friend wants her birthday photos posted?
scenarios.relearn: When unsure something's okay, ask rather than assume.

options.text: Ask: "okay to put these up?"
options.consequence: She picks which ones; all happy.

options.text: Post; she'll probably be fine
options.consequence: 'Probably fine' is a guess, not a yes.

options.text: Post, remove if she minds
options.consequence: By then it's already shared unasked.

scenarios.debrief: Unsure means ask first, not apologise later.

scenarios.hook: Your friend says he has to head home and stop the game.
scenarios.relearn: When someone sets a time boundary, let them go without guilt.

options.text: "Sure, see you tomorrow."
options.consequence: He leaves easy; he'll play again.

options.text: "Real friends would stay."
options.consequence: That's a guilt trick, not a fact.

options.text: Hide his shoes
options.consequence: Blocking him is the opposite of respect.

scenarios.debrief: A time boundary is real; you don't guilt someone for going.

scenarios.hook: At the gurudwara, an elder says she'd rather rest than be helped up.
scenarios.relearn: Even meaning to help, you respect a clear 'I'm fine, thanks'.

options.text: "Of course," and bring water
options.consequence: She feels respected, not handled.

options.text: Lift her up to be helpful
options.consequence: Helping past her 'no' is overriding.

options.text: Insist she not sit so long
options.consequence: Her body, her call; don't argue it.

scenarios.debrief: Good intentions don't let you ignore someone's 'I'm fine'.

scenarios.hook: A friend says she's not in the mood to chat right now.
scenarios.relearn: You can accept a 'not now' warmly without sulking.

yourLine.text: "Totally fine, I'm around when you are."
"Wow, okay, be like that then."

scenarios.hook: You want to look at the drawing your friend is keeping covered.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before peeking at someone's private work.

yourLine.text: "Can I see it, or is it private?"
Lift the cover to peek

scenarios.hook: A friend told you a secret and you almost shared it.
scenarios.relearn: Owning a near-slip and recommitting respects their trust.

yourLine.text: "I nearly told someone, I'm sorry, it stays with me."
"It's not a big deal, everyone gossips."

scenarios.hook: You notice your sister wants to be left alone in her room.
scenarios.relearn: Knock and ask before entering someone's space.

yourLine.text: "Can I come in, or do you want space?"
Walk straight in and flop on her bed

scenarios.hook: Aarav wants to add a quieter classmate to the gaming voice chat.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before pulling someone into a new space online.

yourLine.text: "Want me to add you, or would you rather not?"
Add him without asking and tag him

scenarios.hook: A friend asks you to stop sending so many messages late at night.
scenarios.relearn: Respect a 'message me less'; it's a time boundary, not rejection.

yourLine.text: "Got it, I'll text in the day instead."
"But what if it's important to me?"

scenarios.hook: You're about to retell a friend's embarrassing fall to the class.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before sharing someone's embarrassing moment; their story, their call.

yourLine.text: "Mind if I tell them, or keep it between us?"
Tell the whole class for a laugh

scenarios.hook: Your friend says she doesn't want help with her maths and wants to try alone.
scenarios.relearn: Respect 'I want to try myself'; offer, don't take over.

yourLine.text: "Okay, shout if you want a hand."
Grab her pencil and solve it for her

scenarios.hook: "If I say sorry after, I can do whatever I want first."
scenarios.relearn: Asking first respects a boundary; sorry-after doesn't undo crossing it.

myth.un: A sorry afterward makes it fine to cross someone's boundary.
myth.re: You ask first; a sorry can't un-cross a line you already crossed.
myth.why: Respect happens before the action, not as a clean-up after.

scenarios.hook: "If they don't say no out loud, they're okay with it."
scenarios.relearn: Silence or pulling away isn't a yes; you check in.

myth.un: No words means they're fine with whatever I'm doing.
myth.re: Silence or backing away can mean 'stop'; you check, not assume.
myth.why: People freeze or go quiet; a real yes is clear, not guessed.

scenarios.hook: "Respecting someone's no makes me look soft."
scenarios.relearn: Respecting a no is strong and decent, not weak.

myth.un: Backing off when someone says no makes me look weak.
myth.re: Respecting a no is what strong, decent people do.
myth.why: It takes more strength to honour a line than to bulldoze it.

scenarios.hook: "She's my best friend, so I don't need to ask."
scenarios.relearn: Closeness doesn't cancel asking; best friends still get a say.

myth.un: Being close means I can skip asking my best friend.
myth.re: Even your closest friend gets asked; closeness isn't a free pass.
myth.why: Friendship is built on asking, not on assuming a yes.

scenarios.hook: "If I keep asking, they'll finally say yes, and that's allowed."
scenarios.relearn: A 'yes' worn down by pestering isn't real respect for their no.

myth.un: Asking over and over until they give in is fair game.
myth.re: Wearing someone down isn't a free yes; their first no stood.
myth.why: Pestering pressures a yes; a respected no doesn't need re-asking.

scenarios.hook: "Boys don't have to ask before joining in."
scenarios.relearn: Everyone asks and respects, all genders, no exceptions.

myth.un: Boys can just jump in without asking; that's how boys are.
myth.re: Everyone asks first, boys included; nobody gets a skip.
myth.why: Asking and respecting are for all of us, not a girls-only rule.

scenarios.hook: "It's only respect if the person is older or important."
scenarios.relearn: You respect everyone's boundary, including a younger sibling's.

myth.un: Only big or important people's boundaries need respecting.
myth.re: A younger kid's boundary counts as much as an elder's.
myth.why: Respect isn't about rank; every person's line is real.

scenarios.hook: "If I was just joking, crossing a boundary doesn't count."
scenarios.relearn: A boundary holds even when you meant it as a joke.

myth.un: It doesn't count if I crossed the line as a joke.
myth.re: A line you crossed still counts, joke or not; you stop.
myth.why: What matters is how they feel, not how funny you found it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that ignore someone's boundary.
scenarios.relearn: Asking, knocking, and waiting respect a line; grabbing and prying cross it.

scene.text: Asking before borrowing a charger
Reading a friend's texts over their shoulder
Knocking before opening the door
Taking a snack from a bag without asking
Waiting for a yes before tagging a photo

scenarios.why: Reading their texts and taking without asking skip the other person's say.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two body cues that mean 'back off and check in'.
scenarios.relearn: Pulling away or crossing arms means pause; a smile and lean-in mean comfy.

scene.text: They lean in and keep chatting
They step back and fold their arms
They smile and pass you the ball
They go quiet and turn their body away
They laugh and ask you to stay

scenarios.why: Stepping back, folding arms, going quiet and turning away are 'give me space' cues.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two replies that pressure a 'no' instead of accepting it.
scenarios.relearn: Accepting a no sounds easy; guilt-trips and re-asking are pressure.

scene.text: "No worries, maybe next time."
"If you were my friend you'd say yes."
"Okay, your call."
"Come on, please, please, please?"
"Sure, thanks for telling me."

scenarios.why: The guilt-trip and the begging both push a no instead of respecting it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two moves that skip digital consent.
scenarios.relearn: Ask before posting or tagging others; sharing your own stuff is fine.

scene.text: Asking before tagging a friend
Posting a group photo no one okayed
Sharing a drawing you made yourself
Forwarding a friend's selfie without asking
Checking it's okay before adding someone to a chat

scenarios.why: Posting the unokayed photo and forwarding the selfie both skip the other person's yes.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two ways someone respects a friend who wants space.
scenarios.relearn: Giving space while staying warm respects a 'not now'; prying and sulking don't.

scene.text: "I'm here when you're ready."
Asking again and again why they're upset
Giving them quiet and a kind smile
Sulking so they feel bad for needing space
Sitting nearby without making them talk

scenarios.why: Pestering for a reason and sulking both push past the space they asked for.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that respect a younger sibling's boundary.
scenarios.relearn: Younger siblings get respect too; knocking and asking count for them as well.

scene.text: Knocking before entering his room
Taking his toy because you're older
Asking before borrowing his book
Tickling him after he says stop
Stopping the game when he says he's done

scenarios.why: Taking his toy and ignoring his 'stop' cross his boundary just because he's younger.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two replies that respect someone's 'I'd rather not be touched'.
scenarios.relearn: A wave or a smile respects a no-touch wish; grabbing and guilt don't.

scene.text: Greeting them with a wave instead
Hugging them anyway, just quickly
Saying "sure, a smile works!"
"You'll hurt my feelings if you don't."
Offering a fist bump and moving on

scenarios.why: The quick hug and the guilt line both ignore their no-touch boundary.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respecting a friend's 'not now' is its own kind of caring. What lands for you?
scenarios.relearn: Respecting a 'not now' is a way of showing you care.
scenarios.affirm: Letting someone have their 'not now' is a quiet, real way to care.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: asking 'is this okay?' before touching or sharing feels good both ways. Notice it?
scenarios.relearn: Asking first feels good for both people.
scenarios.affirm: A small 'is this okay?' makes both of you feel safe and seen.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a friend's no isn't about you, it's just their line. Sit with that?
scenarios.relearn: A no is their boundary, not a rejection of you.
scenarios.affirm: A no is just where their line sits; you can let it be without taking it personally.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: reading when a friend wants space is a skill you can grow. Worth practising?
scenarios.relearn: Reading cues for space is a skill you can build.
scenarios.affirm: Noticing when to give space is a skill, and you're already practising it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respecting people you're close to, not just strangers, says a lot. Agree?
scenarios.relearn: Respect counts most with the people closest to you.
scenarios.affirm: Respecting the people nearest you, not just strangers, is the real test, and you've got it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when you're unsure if something's okay with someone, asking beats guessing. Feel that?
scenarios.relearn: When unsure, ask instead of guessing.
scenarios.affirm: Choosing to ask when you're unsure is the kind, clear move every time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you don't need a reason to respect someone's no, you just do. Sit with it?
scenarios.relearn: A no needs no reason to be respected.
scenarios.affirm: A no stands on its own; you respect it whether or not you know why.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: backing off when someone wants space takes strength, not weakness. True for you?
scenarios.relearn: Backing off when asked is strength, not weakness.
scenarios.affirm: Stepping back when someone asks is a strong, grown-up thing to do.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the way you'd want your boundaries handled is how you can handle theirs. Fair?
scenarios.relearn: Handle others' boundaries the way you'd want yours handled.
scenarios.affirm: Treating their lines the way you'd want yours treated keeps things fair and kind.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: noticing a quiet friend and easing off the joke is a real kindness. Notice it?
scenarios.relearn: Easing off when a friend goes quiet is real kindness.
scenarios.affirm: Catching a friend's quiet and easing off is exactly the kind of friend people trust.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: respecting boundaries doesn't make friendships distant, it makes them safe. Agree?
scenarios.relearn: Respecting boundaries makes friendships safer, not distant.
scenarios.affirm: Respect doesn't push friends apart; it's what makes them feel safe with you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when a friend takes back a 'yes', letting them is part of respect. Sit with that?
scenarios.relearn: People can change their mind; letting them is respect.
scenarios.affirm: Letting a friend take back a yes, no fuss, is a clear act of respect.
